newsitem.title: USA: Salt and pepper shakers can spice up gift-giving.
newsitem.headline: Salt and pepper shakers can spice up gift-giving.

text.p: If you want to spice up gift giving this holiday season, salt and pepper shakers may be the thing. Antique glass sets and ceramic novelty items have become true collectors items, experts in the field said.
While very rare salt and pepper shakers from the mid- to late 1800s can fetch $5,000 or more, many sets can still be found for under $40, and some go for even less.
What's more, they are small and easy to store, require little maintenance and can be resold without much trouble, collectors and experts said.
But most of all to the collectors, older salt and pepper shakers are things of great beauty.
"I just love old glass," said Janice Eldridge, a great-grandmother in Springfield, Mass., who started collecting 10 years ago. "The art glass forms are just beautiful."

"You don't see that in salt shakers today. You get a hunk of plastic on the table today," said Ralph Lechner, a Virginia-based collector and co-author, with his wife, of "The World of Salt Shakers" (Collector Books, $24.95).

Eldridge had no idea she would come to own 400 salt and pepper sets when she started going to auctions a decade ago. She was out to find a display case for some old family glassware after her mother came to live with her in 1981.
"I wanted to put it in a china cabinet to make her feel at home, like we had up in Maine on the farm," said Eldridge, 71, whose mother died in 1993.
While hunting for the cabinet, salt and pepper shakers caught her eye. Eldridge bought a Victorian "bulging petal" model and three other sets at auction, and she was hooked.

The cabinet for the family glassware? She found it. She stores some of her porcelain in it today. In addition to her private stock, Eldridge has another 700 sets and constantly buys, sells and swaps with collectors and other dealers.
Lechner started collecting with his wife, Mildred, in the 1950s. They keep buying for the love of the items, but have found, too, that prices have kept rising.
"They just go up gradually over the years," Lechner, 72, said by telephone from his home in Mechanicsville, Va.

A pair of Christmas "opalware" salt and pepper shakers that fetches $175 today cost about $40 in the 1960s, when the Lechner's collection was small. They have more than 1,500 sets today. Opalware refers to a milky type of glass.
An extremely rare "peach blow" set made by the Mount Washington Glass Co. in the 1880s can fetch $5,000 or more, depending on decoration, Lechner said.
"Collectors go absolutely nuts over it. Only a couple thousand individual pieces were made, and people were probably throwing away stuff like that after the Depression."
Peach blow was a marketing term used by manufacturers to refer to the smoothness of the glass. Many late 19th century salt shakers were hand-blown by skilled artisans.

Companies constantly copied designs, which can sometimes make identifying a manufacturer difficult. Collectible sets were made by New England Glass Co., Imperial Glass Co., Eagle Glass & Manufacturing Co., and C.F. Monroe Co., experts said.
Glass salt and pepper shakers are not the only kinds to collect. Ceramic sets have become popular and they too are rising in price.

A pair of brown & white spaniel shakers made by Ceramic Arts Studio, now defunct, sold for $375 at a convention last year, according to Irene Thornburg, a collector who worked for Kellogg Co. for 31 years until she retired in 1987.

"Maybe 10 years ago, you probably could have bought them for about $15," said Thornburg, 66, who counts more than 14,000 pairs in her collection, stored in a barn her husband built several years back.
Of course, not all sets have appreciated as rapidly.

The first two that Thornburg bought in 1949 on a trip to Florida with her parents were an ear of corn and a bunch of celery. Cost then: maybe 29 cents a pair. Value now: $2 to $3 a pair in the Midwest, slightly higher on either coast.

An experience Thornburg had at a flea market a few years back shows that it pays to know what you're looking for. She paid $2 for a pair of hugging pigs designed by Ruth Bendel (nee van Tellingen) for Regal China. They turned out to be worth $250.
"I just couldn't believe it, they were all out there, all kinds. You sort of have to be very nonchalant," she said.

Her advice: buy what you like. "If you see it and you like it, buy it. Most people getting started get bit by the bug and buy everything in sight," she said, noting people often end up focusing on one or more areas.
Lechner and his wife specialise in Victorian era shakers, for example. Eldridge concentrates on glass shakers from C.F. Monroe, known as Wave Crest, and Mount Washington.
For more information, contact the Novelty Salt & Pepper Shakers Club at 561 588-5368 and the Antique & Art Glass Salt Shaker Collectors' Society at 407 629-1168. Both clubs publish newsletters.
